title: Safety audit: safe public Stream::open permits forgetting borrowed work
body:
`throughput::Stream::open` remains public and safe, though doc-hidden. A safe-Rust function compiles that opens it, submits borrowed input/output, calls `mem::forget(stream)`, then overwrites/frees those buffers. Published tasks can retain their raw pointers. Drop and the outer stream function's abort-on-unwind scope are both bypassed.

**The witness was type-checked only, never called: no dangling task or freed-buffer access was executed.** It is in a separate public-API probe crate on exact ddb7199d7f0b0f04390e923474b630ffc7ff2811. open/submit and the implicated borrowed-storage contract are unchanged from next fbfb319f3414ac7fac4b3d4bce266488a1fdee3b.

A safe guard cannot require its destructor for memory safety: forgetting it may leak resources but must preserve Rust soundness. The scoped `throughput::stream` call already supplies the intended ownership mechanism. Repository search finds open's only Rust call in that function; the current convenience-only C API has no call. The doc's C-API justification appears vestigial after #279.

Smallest remedy to review: make open private and remove its obsolete C-API wording, retaining the existing scoped entry. A compile-fail check should reject this direct constructor witness; ordinary scoped-stream examples should continue working. No new stream implementation/API concept is needed.

Pinned evidence: safety-cursory-probes-epyc-20261108T144442-53674417; full script/raw publication follows. This is a source-level safety argument with an accepted compile witness, not a dynamically reproduced UAF. Please review as a separate safety blocker beside the ring fix.

— Sam Shackleton
